levels.title: You
levels.subtitle: The center of your entire universe.
facts: Atom Count: Your body is composed of approximately 7 octillion atoms (mostly hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, and nitrogen).
Stellar Origin: Every heavier atom in your body (iron, calcium, phosphorus) was forged inside ancient dying stars billions of years ago.
Older Than Stars: Roughly 60% of your atoms are hydrogen, and every single one of them has existed since the Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago.
Mostly Nothing: Atoms are about 99.9999999999% empty space. Squeeze that emptiness out and all 8 billion humans would fit inside a sugar cube.
Borrowed Mass: Around 99% of your mass isn't from the particles themselves. It's the pure energy of quarks and gluons buzzing inside every proton and neutron.
Bio-Electricity: Your brain runs on about 20 watts of power, dimmer than a bulb, yet it outperforms supercomputers drawing millions of watts at certain tasks.
Cellular Turnover: Every day, your body produces around 300 billion new cells to replace dead or damaged tissue.
Not Just You: You carry roughly 38 trillion microbes, about as many bacterial cells as human cells. You are an ecosystem, not an individual.
Solar Neutrinos: Trillions of invisible neutrinos streaming from the Sun pass through your body every second without stopping.
DNA Stretch: Uncoil all the DNA in your cells and it would stretch over 70 billion km, enough to reach Pluto and back about six times.
Thermal Glow: Your body radiates heat in the infrared spectrum; if our eyes could see infrared, you would glow in total darkness.
Single-Photon Eyes: Your retinal rod cells can react to a single photon of light, the smallest possible packet of light.
Ancient Sunlight: The energy in every meal you eat is sunlight captured by plants, sometimes only weeks ago, sometimes (for fossil-fed crops) from the ancient past.
Atom Recycling: Most of the atoms in you today were not in you a few years ago. You are a pattern that keeps swapping out its own material.
Time Warp: Your head ages slightly faster than your feet, because gravity is weaker higher up. Over a lifetime the gap is about half a millionth of a second.
Interstellar Water: Over 60% of your body is water, and a large share of its hydrogen formed before the Solar System even existed.

levels.title: Your World
levels.subtitle: Your entire existence, cradled in blue.
facts: Immediate Horizon: At 10 kilometers across, this represents your daily physical footprint and immediate atmospheric sphere.
Troposphere: Within this scale lies the troposphere, containing about 75% of Earth's atmospheric mass and virtually all weather systems.
Human Perspective: For most of human history, an individual's entire known world fit within this single scale stop.
The Weight of Air: A column of air presses on every square centimeter of you with about 1 kg of force. Your body carries roughly 15 tonnes of atmosphere and you never feel it.
Everest in the Ocean: The Mariana Trench is about 10.9 km deep. Drop Mount Everest into it and the summit would still be over 2 km underwater.
How Far You See: Standing on flat ground, your horizon is only about 4.7 km away. Your whole visible world is smaller than this level.
Caesar's Breath: A single breath holds so many molecules that you very likely inhale a few that were exhaled by Julius Caesar.
Dust From Space: Tens of tons of cosmic dust settle onto Earth every day. Some of what you sweep off a windowsill is stardust.
Soil Universe: A teaspoon of healthy soil contains about as many microbes as there are people on Earth.
Sound Barrier: Sound travels across this 10 km horizon in about 30 seconds under normal atmospheric conditions.
Visual Curvature: From the top of this scale, the subtle curvature of the Earth begins to become faintly perceptible.
Atmospheric Pressure: Air pressure drops by half roughly every 5.5 kilometers you ascend within this boundary.

levels.title: Earth
levels.subtitle: A pale blue speck suspended in a sunbeam.
levels.sizeFact: Sunlight takes 8 min 20 s to arrive
facts: Orbital Velocity: Earth races around the Sun at about 107,000 km/h while spinning at 1,670 km/h at the equator.
Water vs Mass: 71% of Earth's surface is covered in water, yet water makes up only about 0.02% of Earth's total mass.
Protective Shield: Earth's molten iron outer core generates a magnetosphere that deflects lethal solar wind and cosmic radiation.
Atmospheric Thinness: If Earth were a basketball, the breathable atmosphere would be thinner than the skin of an apple.
Hot Heart: Earth's solid inner core is a ball of iron roughly three-quarters the size of the Moon, as hot as the surface of the Sun (about 5,400°C).
Squashed Planet: Earth bulges at the equator, so the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is farther from Earth's center than the peak of Everest.
Life Underground: Microbes live kilometers beneath your feet in solid rock, some surviving for thousands to millions of years on almost no energy.
99% Extinct: More than 99% of all species that have ever lived on Earth are now extinct.
Snowball Earth: Around 700 million years ago, Earth may have frozen almost entirely over, with ice reaching the equator.
Lightning Storm: Somewhere on Earth, around 40 to 50 lightning flashes happen every single second.
Slowing Spin: Earth's days are getting longer by about 2 milliseconds per century. Dinosaurs lived on a planet with 23-hour days.
Species Share: Plants make up over 80% of all living biomass. All humans together are only about 0.01%.
Cosmic Calendar: Squash Earth's 4.5 billion years into one year and modern humans appear in the last 35 minutes of December 31.
Continental Drift: Earth's continents drift apart at about 2.5 centimeters per year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow.
Ancient Atmosphere: Early Earth had no free oxygen. Photosynthetic microbes poisoned the old world and built the new one 2.4 billion years ago (the Great Oxidation Event).
Magnetic Flips: Earth's magnetic north and south poles have swapped places hundreds of times in geological history.

levels.title: The Moon
levels.subtitle: Our silent neighbor, watching over our brief history.
facts: Tidal Locking: The Moon rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same face always points toward Earth and one side is never seen from here.
Drifting Away: Due to tidal friction, the Moon is spiraling away from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters every year.
Cosmic Coincidence: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away. That is why total solar eclipses look perfect, and only in our era.
Eclipses Will End: In roughly 600 million years the Moon will have drifted too far to fully cover the Sun, and total solar eclipses will vanish forever.
Giant Impact: The Moon was born about 4.5 billion years ago when a Mars-sized protoplanet named Theia slammed into the young Earth.
Colder Than Pluto: Some permanently shadowed craters at the Moon's poles drop to about -248°C, colder than Pluto's surface, and they hold billions of years of frozen water.
Gunpowder Smell: Apollo astronauts reported that moon dust smelled like spent gunpowder once it was tracked back into the lander.
Shrinking Moon: The Moon's interior is cooling and the whole body has shrunk by around 50 meters, wrinkling its surface with young cliffs.
Laser Ping: Mirrors left by Apollo astronauts still reflect laser pulses fired from Earth, letting scientists measure the Moon's distance to within millimeters.
Ringing Like a Bell: Apollo seismometers recorded moonquakes that kept shaking for more than ten minutes because the Moon's dry interior barely damps vibrations.
Footprints Forever: Neil Armstrong's footprints will likely last for millions of years. With no wind or rain, only micrometeorites slowly erase them.
Twelve Humans: Only twelve people have ever walked on the Moon. No human has been back since 1972.
Stabilizing Axis: The Moon's gravity steadies Earth's axial tilt, preventing extreme, chaotic climate swings over geologic time.
Extreme Temperatures: Lunar surface temperatures swing from 127°C in direct sunlight to -173°C in the dark, over a distance of a few meters.

levels.title: The Sun
levels.subtitle: Our raging nuclear furnace fueling every breath you take.
facts: Solar Mass: The Sun accounts for 99.86% of all the mass in the entire solar system.
A Million Earths: The Sun's volume could hold about 1.3 million Earths.
Nuclear Fusion: Every second, the core fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, converting about 4 million tons of matter directly into energy.
Surprisingly Gentle Core: Per cubic meter, the Sun's core produces about as much power as a compost heap. It is powerful only because it is unimaginably huge.
Blazing Core: Temperatures at the solar core reach about 15 million°C, while the visible surface (photosphere) is a relatively cool 5,500°C.
The Hot Corona Mystery: The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, is over a million degrees, hundreds of times hotter than the surface below it. Why? Scientists are still working it out.
Light Travel: A photon created in the core takes tens of thousands to 100,000+ years to bounce its way to the surface, then only 8 minutes to reach Earth.
Solid Gas: The core's plasma is about 150 times denser than water, around eight times denser than gold, yet it behaves like a gas.
Fastest Machine: In 2024, NASA's Parker Solar Probe skimmed 6.1 million km from the Sun at about 692,000 km/h, the fastest human-made object ever.
One Hour of Sun: The sunlight hitting Earth in a single hour holds about as much energy as all of humanity uses in a year.
Carrington Event: In 1859, a solar storm was so powerful that telegraph operators got electric shocks and sparks set their paper on fire.
Almost Perfect Sphere: The Sun is rounder than any natural object we can measure, with a pole-to-equator difference of only about 10 km across 1.39 million km.
Brighter Over Time: The young Sun was about 30% dimmer. It keeps brightening, and in about a billion years Earth's oceans will begin to boil away.
Red Giant Fate: In about 5 billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant and swallow Mercury and Venus, and may reach Earth.
Sound Waves: The Sun rings like a giant bell with acoustic waves, and astronomers read its interior by listening to those vibrations (helioseismology).
Sunspot Cycles: Every 11 years the Sun's magnetic poles flip, triggering intense solar flares and auroral storms on Earth.

levels.title: Our Solar System
levels.subtitle: 8 worlds dancing in the void. V1 & V2 blink back from the dark.
levels.sizeFact: Voyager 1 & 2: ~24 and ~20 light-hours deep in interstellar space
facts: Voyager Legacy: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is humanity's most distant emissary, nearly 26 billion km from home and soon to cross one full light-day away.
Voyager 2, The Grand Tourist: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989). It exploited a planetary alignment that happens only once every ~175 years.
Launch Order Twist: Voyager 2 actually launched first, on August 20, 1977. Voyager 1 left two weeks later but took a faster path and overtook it.
Leaving the Bubble: Voyager 2 crossed the edge of the Sun's heliosphere in November 2018, about 18 billion km out, and began sampling the plasma of interstellar space.
Voyager 2's Discoveries: It found ten new moons of Uranus, volcano-like geysers on Neptune's moon Triton, and a storm on Neptune the size of Earth, the Great Dark Spot.
The Cosmic Shout: In 2023, a wrong antenna command left Voyager 2 pointing away from Earth and silent for about two weeks. NASA revived it by blasting a command across 20 billion km.
Dying Batteries of Stardust: Both Voyagers run on plutonium that loses about 4 watts of power per year. Engineers switch off instruments one by one to keep them alive into the 2030s.
Messages in Bottles: Each Voyager carries a golden record with greetings in 55 languages, music, and sounds of Earth, a time capsule that will outlast Earth itself.
Whisper From the Dark: Voyager's radio sends only about 23 watts, and by the time it reaches Earth the signal is roughly a billion-billionth of a watt. We still hear it.
Venus Oddity: A day on Venus (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 Earth days), and the Sun rises in the west.
Saturn Would Float: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. In a bathtub big enough, it would float.
Biggest Volcano: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 22 km tall, roughly two and a half times the height of Everest.
Endless Storm: Jupiter's Great Red Spot has been raging for at least 190 years and is still wider than Earth.
Hidden Oceans: Jupiter's moon Europa probably holds more liquid water beneath its ice than all of Earth's oceans combined.
Supersonic Winds: Neptune's winds reach about 2,000 km/h, the fastest in the solar system, driven by a planet that is barely warmed by the Sun.
Pluto's Long Year: Pluto takes 248 Earth years to orbit the Sun. It will not complete its first orbit since its 1930 discovery until 2178.
Moon Destined to Break: Mars's moon Phobos is spiraling inward and will be torn into a ring in 30 to 50 million years.
Interstellar Visitors: Three objects from other star systems have been caught passing through: 'Oumuamua (2017), Borisov (2019), and 3I/ATLAS (2025).
Oort Cloud: The solar system's gravitational boundary extends into the Oort Cloud, nearly 2 light-years out, about halfway to the nearest star.
Orbital Plane: All eight planets orbit in nearly the same flat plane, a relic of the spinning disk of gas and dust that formed them 4.6 billion years ago.
Gas Giants: Jupiter and Saturn contain more than 90% of the planetary mass orbiting the Sun.
Heliosphere: The Sun blows a giant magnetic bubble that shields the inner planets from galactic cosmic rays.
Planetary Migration: Evidence suggests Jupiter and Saturn wandered through the solar system in its chaotic youth, flinging comets and rearranging worlds.

levels.title: The Milky Way
levels.subtitle: 400 billion stars. You are invisible from here.
facts: Stellar Empire: The Milky Way contains between 100 and 400 billion stars and at least as many planets.
Supermassive Heart: At the galactic center lies Sagittarius A*, a black hole 4 million times the mass of our Sun, photographed directly in 2022.
Stars on the Edge: The star S2 whips around Sagittarius A* at about 7,650 km/s, roughly 2.5% of the speed of light.
Galactic Year: Our solar system takes about 230 million years to circle the galactic center once. Last time we were here, dinosaurs were just emerging.
Dark Matter Halo: Around 85-90% of the Milky Way's mass is invisible dark matter, which we detect only by its gravity.
Other Earths: Estimates suggest around 1 in 5 Sun-like stars could host an Earth-size planet in the habitable zone. That could mean billions of candidate worlds.
Galactic Cannibal: The Milky Way is eating the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy right now and swallowed a massive galaxy (Gaia-Enceladus) about 10 billion years ago.
Runaway Stars: Black hole encounters have flung hypervelocity stars out at over 1,700 km/s, fast enough to leave the galaxy forever.
Star Nurseries Wave: A 9,000-light-year-long ripple of gas called the Radcliffe Wave carries many of our nearby star-forming regions.
Star Factory: The galaxy forms roughly 1 to 3 Sun-masses of new stars every year, and a star is born somewhere in the Milky Way every few months.
Tiny Neighborhood: The roughly 5,000 stars visible to your naked eye all lie within just a few thousand light-years, a minuscule corner of the galaxy.
Gaia's Census: The Gaia space telescope has mapped the positions and motions of nearly 2 billion stars, building a 3D movie of our galaxy.
High-Speed Travel: The solar system orbits the galactic center at about 828,000 km/h.
Spiral Structure: Our galaxy is a barred spiral with major arms where active star formation constantly takes place.
Fermi Bubbles: Colossal gamma-ray bubbles extend about 25,000 light-years above and below the galactic plane, likely remnants of past black hole outbursts.

levels.title: Our Galactic Neighborhood
levels.subtitle: A tiny cluster of island universes drifting in nothingness.
facts: Local Group: Our galaxy belongs to the Local Group, a gravitational club of over 80 galaxies spanning about 10 million light-years.
Andromeda Collision: The Milky Way and Andromeda are approaching each other at about 110 km/s and will merge in roughly 4.5 billion years.
Collision Without Crashes: When they merge, almost no stars will collide. Stars are so far apart that galaxies pass through each other like ghosts. The result is nicknamed Milkomeda.
Andromeda's Glow: Andromeda holds about 1 trillion stars and is visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge. You are seeing light that left it 2.5 million years ago.
Giant in the Sky: If Andromeda were bright enough to see in full, it would span about six full Moons across the night sky.
Next Victim: The Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy, is falling toward the Milky Way and is expected to merge with it in about 2.4 billion years.
Dark Galaxies: The dwarf galaxy Segue 1 holds about 3,000 times more mass in dark matter than in visible stars.
Galaxy Speed: The Local Group as a whole is moving at about 630 km/s relative to the afterglow of the Big Bang.
Triangulum Galaxy: M33 is the third-largest member of the Local Group, spinning with about 40 billion stars.
Dwarf Companions: Giant spirals (Milky Way and Andromeda) are accompanied by dozens of tiny dwarf galaxies.
Crowded vs Empty: Andromeda is only about 25 Milky Way-widths away. Galaxies are spaced far closer than stars, which is why they collide and merge so often.
Dark Matter Dominance: Visible stars account for less than 5% of the total mass of the Local Group; the rest is invisible dark matter.

levels.title: The Laniakea Supercluster
levels.subtitle: Rivers of 100,000 galaxies flowing together toward a massive gravitational basin.
levels.sizeFact: 520 million light-years across · Home to the Great Attractor
facts: Laniakea Meaning: Hawaiian for 'Immeasurable Heaven', Laniakea defines the huge region of galaxies that flow together toward the same point in space.
Our Cosmic Address: The Milky Way sits on the outskirts of the Virgo Supercluster, which turns out to be just one small branch of Laniakea.
The Great Attractor: Laniakea's 100,000 galaxies, including ours, are sliding along gravitational streamlines toward a titanic gravitational anomaly.
Hidden by Our Own Galaxy: Much of the Great Attractor's region is hidden behind the Milky Way's dust and stars. This 'Zone of Avoidance' blocks about 20% of the sky.
Pushed Away, Too: Besides being pulled, we are also being pushed. A vast, nearly empty region called the Dipole Repeller is shoving galaxies away from it.
Quadrillion Suns: Laniakea contains about 10^17 solar masses, one hundred quadrillion times the mass of our Sun.
Water Flowing Downhill: Laniakea is defined like a watershed. Galaxies flow inward along its 'rivers' the way rain collects in a river basin.
Temporary Structure: Dark energy is accelerating the universe's expansion so strongly that Laniakea is not permanently bound and may eventually come apart.
Mapping the Invisible: Laniakea was mapped with peculiar velocities, measuring how each galaxy's motion deviates from the smooth cosmic expansion.

levels.title: The Cosmic Web
levels.subtitle: Galaxies strung together like fragile glowing webs.
facts: Cosmic Neural Network: Galaxies are arranged in vast intersecting filaments, and studies find the web's structure looks strikingly similar to the network of neurons in a brain.
Cosmic Voids: Between the filaments lie immense dark voids hundreds of millions of light-years across and nearly empty of galaxies.
The Boötes Void: One void, about 330 million light-years wide, holds only around 60 galaxies where roughly 2,000 would be expected.
Dark Matter Scaffolding: The glowing web of galaxies is merely the frosting on an invisible scaffold of dark matter.
Missing Matter Found: For decades, about half of all ordinary matter was missing. It turned out to be hiding in thin, hot, invisible threads of the cosmic web.
Photographing the Web: In 2014, a quasar lit up a filament of hydrogen gas about 2 million light-years long, the first direct image of a thread of the web.
Super Walls: The Sloan Great Wall of galaxies stretches about 1.4 billion light-years, and the Giant Arc stretches 3.3 billion, challenging the idea that the universe is smooth at large scales.
Emptier Than Empty: Averaged across the cosmos, matter is about one atom per four cubic meters, billions of times emptier than the best vacuum we can build on Earth.
Spinning Along Threads: Galaxies tend to spin in alignment with the filaments they are embedded in, as if the web gave them their twist.
Filament Intersections: Where filaments intersect, they form rich superclusters containing thousands of galaxies.
Acoustic Relics: The web's honeycomb pattern was seeded by quantum ripples in the early universe, then shaped by sound waves in the primordial plasma.

levels.title: The Observable Universe
levels.subtitle: ~2 trillion galaxies (conservative estimate). Beyond lies the infinite unknown.
levels.sizeFact: We only see what light has reached. Beyond, realms exist in eternal shadow.
facts: Galaxy Count: Deep field observations by Hubble and James Webb suggest the observable universe holds trillions of galaxies.
Cosmic Microwave Background: The oldest light in existence, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, blankets every inch of the sky at a temperature of 2.7 K.
Old TV Static: A small percentage of the snow on an old analog TV was the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.
Only 5%: Everything we can see, every star, planet, and gas cloud, is only about 5% of the universe. Roughly 27% is dark matter and 68% is dark energy.
Observable Diameter: The observable universe is roughly 93 billion light-years across despite being only 13.8 billion years old, because space itself has been expanding.

Beyond Reach: Even if you left today at light speed, you could only ever reach galaxies within about 16 billion light-years. The vast majority of the observable universe is already unreachable forever.
Cosmic Amnesia: In the far future, expansion will push all other galaxies beyond view. Astronomers then will see only their own galaxy and have no evidence for the Big Bang.
Early Giants: JWST has found galaxies that already existed less than 300 million years after the Big Bang, earlier and brighter than theories predicted.
Expansion Mystery: Two precise ways of measuring how fast the universe expands disagree (about 67 vs 73 km/s per megaparsec). Something may be missing from physics.
Atom Count: The observable universe contains roughly 10^80 atoms, a 1 followed by 80 zeros.
Why Night Is Dark: The night sky is dark because the universe has a beginning. If it were infinitely old, every line of sight would end on a star.
Superluminal Expansion: Space itself can expand faster than light, meaning distant galaxies are permanently receding beyond our horizon.
Stellar Count: There are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches combined (about 10^22 to 10^24).

levels.title: Beyond the Observable Universe
levels.subtitle: Where light has never touched, and space stretches into the infinite.
levels.sizeFact: An endless tapestry beyond our cosmic light horizon
facts: The Light Horizon: Because light has only had 13.8 billion years to travel to us, everything beyond about 46.5 billion light-years is hidden. Not because nothing is there, but because light hasn't had time to arrive.

Seemingly Flat: Measurements show the universe is flat to within a fraction of a percent. Like the Earth looks flat up close, that suggests the whole is far larger than what we can see, perhaps infinite.
Inflation: In the first 10^-32 seconds, space is thought to have stretched by a factor of at least 10^26. Our whole observable universe may be one tiny patch of that expansion.
Eternal Inflation: In many models inflation never fully stops. It keeps spawning new bubble universes, each possibly with different physics.
Causality Barrier: Beyond our horizon, space recedes faster than light, creating a cosmic curtain that isolates our region from whatever lies beyond.

Doppelgangers: If space is infinite and matter is spread randomly, then somewhere, about 10^(10^28) meters away by one estimate, there could be a region identical to ours, including another you reading this.

Wraparound Universe: The universe could be finite but have no edge, like a video game map that wraps around. Travel far enough in a straight line and you might arrive back where you started. So far, we see no evidence of it.
The Worst Prediction: Quantum theory predicts the energy of empty space to be up to 10^120 times larger than what we observe. It is the biggest mismatch in all of physics.
Multiverse Possibilities: In an infinite expanding space, pocket universes and alternate histories could repeat endlessly across the quantum landscape.
